Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: A family holiday is approaching, which is a traditional time for everyone to reconnect.
Expectation2: Greet clients and make them feel comfortable
Situation2: A bride-to-be and her entourage arrive early, visibly anxious about the tight wedding schedule.
Story: The salon was already buzzing when I glanced at my phone and saw a message from my daughter: “Don’t forget, we’re all meeting on the video call at noon to plan the holiday dinner!” My heart squeezed a little. Family holidays were sacred, a time when I was expected to help keep everyone connected, to be the glue that held us together. But just then, the door chimed and in swept the bride and her bridesmaids, all nerves and excitement, an hour earlier than expected. As a hairdresser, I knew my job was to greet them warmly, put them at ease, and make sure their special day started perfectly. I could see the tension in their faces, the way the bride twisted her hands. I wanted to give them my full attention, to be the calm in their storm. But my phone buzzed again—a reminder of my other role, the one that needed me to be present for my family, to help plan a holiday that meant so much to all of us. I stood there, scissors in hand, torn between the expectations of my family and my clients, feeling the weight of both worlds pressing in.
